issues.legal_issue: A litigant seeking discretionary writ relief must disclose material prior proceedings, and suppression of those proceedings permits dismissal without consideration of the merits.
material_facts: The appellants sought writ relief concerning allotments over land they claimed had not been acquired.
Before filing the writ petition, they had brought a civil suit raising substantially the same claim, and that suit had been dismissed; the appeal from that dismissal had also been dismissed.
The appellants did not disclose the suit, its dismissal, or the dismissal of the appeal in their writ petition.
issues.conclusion: The appellants had not approached the court with clean hands and were not entitled to extraordinary, equitable, and discretionary relief; the writ claim could be dismissed for suppression without deciding its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution is extraordinary, equitable, and discretionary. A petitioner must candidly disclose all material facts; suppression or misleading presentation can warrant dismissal without consideration of the merits. The Court relied on Prestige Lights Ltd. v. State Bank of India, Udyami Evam Khadi Gramodyog Welfare Sanstha v. State of Uttar Pradesh, K.D. Sharma v. Steel Authority of India Ltd., and the principle stated in R. v. Kensington Income Tax Commissioners.

predicates.writ_proceeding: The claimant sought discretionary relief from a court exercising writ jurisdiction.
predicates.prior_related_litigation_exists: The claimant had previously pursued a legal proceeding concerning the same or a related subject matter.
predicates.prior_litigation_was_not_disclosed: The claimant did not disclose the prior proceeding and its relevant outcome to the court.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks writ relief after pursuing related litigation and does not disclose it, the court may deny writ relief without reviewing the merits.

issues.legal_issue: Parties must disclose known past and present litigation concerning any part of the subject matter, and must state that no such litigation exists when that is their position.
material_facts: The appellants' earlier civil suit and appeal concerned the same disputed land and raised contentions similar to those in their writ petition.
The appellants omitted those proceedings and their outcomes from the writ pleadings.
issues.conclusion: Parties must disclose details of all past or present legal proceedings concerning any part of the disputed subject matter within their knowledge; if they contend that there are none, they must state that in their pleadings.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated this disclosure requirement to prevent multiplicity of proceedings and attempts to obtain inconsistent orders by withholding or misrepresenting litigation history. It accords with the equitable and discretionary character of writ jurisdiction under Article 226 and the candour requirement discussed in Prestige Lights Ltd. v. State Bank of India, Udyami Evam Khadi Gramodyog Welfare Sanstha v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and K.D. Sharma v. Steel Authority of India Ltd.

predicates.court_pleading_involves_disputed_subject: A party filed pleadings asking a court to resolve a dispute about a subject matter.
predicates.party_knows_of_related_legal_proceedings: The party knew of past or present legal proceedings concerning any part of that subject matter.

issues.definition: A party pleading about a disputed subject matter must disclose related proceedings that the party knows about.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that part of acquired land was left unacquired cannot succeed where the whole extent was notified and a final prior judgment has determined that the whole extent was acquired.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications covered the entire survey extent, including the portion claimed by the appellants to have been left out.
The records showed that the disputed eight-gunta portion was kharab-B land, while compensation had been awarded for the revenue-paying portion.
A prior civil suit raising the same contention was dismissed, and the dismissal was confirmed on appeal; the appellate finding that the entire extent had been acquired had become final.
The appellants later raised the same contention in their writ proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The entire extent, including the disputed kharab-B land, had been acquired; no compensation was payable for that kharab-B portion. The final prior appellate finding was binding, and the writ court could not sit in appeal over it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the acquisition notifications and records showing that the whole extent was included and that the disputed portion was kharab-B land, for which compensation was not payable. It also applied the finality of the prior appellate judgment. The earlier appeal had treated the suit as impliedly barred under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure because the acquisition had become final and conclusive. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 18, was part of the compensation-reference history but was not the basis for reopening the acquisition issue.

predicates.acquisition_dispute_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim that land was not included in an acquisition.
predicates.land_extent_included_in_acquisition_noti: The acquisition notifications covered the whole land extent, including the portion later claimed to have been left out.
predicates.disputed_portion_is_kharab_land: The records identify the disputed portion as kharab land for which compensation was not payable.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_determined_entire_e: A final judgment in earlier litigation determined that the acquisition covered the entire extent.

issues.definition: A claim that a portion was left unacquired must be rejected when the notifications covered it, it is kharab land, and a final prior judgment determined that the whole extent was acquired.
